This is the list, and it is the only one in the course. Chapter 3 sent you here for it. Same list for one asset and for a batch of fourteen, run in this order.

1. Open the exported file itself, not the preview panel. Missing fonts, hidden layers, white boxes and transparent backgrounds that turned black show themselves here and nowhere else.
2. Check the piece against your fixed list: margin, logo, contact line, and nothing important sitting out in the outer band.
3. Look at it on a phone at real size, with no zoom.
4. Shrink it to thumbnail size. Is the first thing still first?
5. Read every word out loud, the phone number digit by digit, checked against the client's own message and not your memory of it. Typos survive being looked at and die on being said.
6. If the background is not yours, view it on light and on dark. If it is going on paper, look at the printed proof from reading distance.
7. Confirm the essential information also exists as text outside the image, and write the alt text.
8. Send it with one line saying what it is and where it goes.

Rowena laid out a poster for a dental clinic in Cabanatuan with the schedule in thin light grey, because it looked calm on her laptop. On a phone in a tricycle the schedule was not there at all. The check would have caught it in under a minute.

## Then hand it to someone who has not seen it

You have been inside this file long enough that your eye fills in type too small to read and words half hidden behind a photo.

Give the phone to somebody else, say nothing, and ask two questions. What is this about, and what does it want you to do? If they name something other than the element you ranked first, your ranking is wrong, not their eyesight. Fix the piece rather than explaining it.

## Do this before the next lesson

Run the check on your own piece, on a real phone, and write down what it caught. Then hand the phone to somebody who has not seen the file, say nothing, and ask the two questions. Whatever they name first is what your piece actually leads with, whatever you intended.

lessons.title: AI images, honestly
lessons.content_mdx:
# AI images, honestly

Image generation and AI editing now sit inside the same tools you already use. That makes the technical question easy and the professional question harder. Two things decide it: what these tools are genuinely good at, and what you would be willing to say out loud that you used one for.

Prompt writing itself belongs to the prompt engineering course. This lesson is about judgment.

## What they are good at, as categories

- Backgrounds and texture, where nothing in the picture is a claim.
- Quick variations of a layout idea, so you can pick a direction before committing.
- Removing an object that should not be in the frame, or extending a background so a real photo fits a new shape.
- Cleaning up a usable photo the client sent from a group chat.
- Rough mockups inside an internal draft, labelled as mockups.

The thread running through those: the image is decoration, or it is a working draft nobody will treat as evidence.

## What they wreck

- Hands, teeth, and the edges of a group of people.
- Text inside an image. Signage, packaging, a menu, anything with words in it.
- Logos. A generated logo is a smeared impression of logos it has seen.
- Real people's faces, including a small AI touch-up of a staff photo.
- Any product a customer will actually receive.

One rule covers that last item and saves you a great deal of trouble: if a customer will hold the real thing next to the picture, do not generate the picture.

## The honesty line

This is the part of the lesson worth keeping.

Never generate an image that says something happened. A photo of the product, the storefront, the team, a before and after, a face attached to a testimonial, a queue of customers, a packed event, an award, a certificate. Those are not decoration. They are evidence, and inventing evidence is lying, whatever the tool is called.

A printing shop in Marikina asks Nico for a shot of customers lining up outside, for their anniversary post. There was no line. A generated queue is a claim about demand, and inventing recognisable faces outside a real storefront is worse than the claim. What Nico offers instead: shoot the actual shop on a good afternoon, or drop the crowd photo entirely and let type and colour carry the anniversary offer.

Where the graphic carries a claim of its own, such as a discount, a health or beauty result, or a comparison with a competitor, chapter 1 already told you the move: get the client's written confirmation that it is a claim they are cleared to make, and keep the message. That confirmation matters more here than anywhere else in the course, because a generated image sitting under an unchecked claim is two inventions stacked on one another.

## Disclosure has two audiences

**The client, always.** Every asset carrying generated or AI-edited content gets named in your handover: what was generated, what was edited and how, and which images are real photographs. Ask first, in writing, whether AI generation is allowed on their account at all. Some brands say no, some of their own customers say no, and finding that out after publishing is the expensive order.

**The audience, when the image could be mistaken for a record.** A generated texture behind type needs no label. A person, a place, a product or a result does. And a label does not rescue a dishonest image: writing "AI generated" under a fake queue does not make the queue true.

Say it plainly to the client. "I can generate the background. I will not generate a photo of your product. Send me one shot on a plain table near a window and I will handle the rest."

## What you never upload

- Confidential client material: unreleased designs, price lists, contracts, anything under an agreement.
- A customer's photo, or any private person's face, including a testimonial screenshot with a name on it.
- A staff photo without written permission from the person in it.
- Anything you would be uncomfortable seeing in a competitor's advertisement.

Whether a vendor stores or learns from what you upload differs by product and by account tier, and it changes. Reading the current terms for the specific tool you are using is part of the job.

## Rights are unsettled, so ask the questions first

Nobody can tell you today what a generated image is worth as property, and the answer differs by vendor and by country. That is not a reason to avoid the tools. It is a reason to ask three questions before generated work goes anywhere paid.

What do this tool's current terms say about commercial use on this account? What does the client's own agreement say about AI content? Can I state on the record exactly what was generated?

If you cannot answer all three, it does not go on paid work.

## Do this before the assignment

Write your disclosure now, before you make anything: what you generated, what you AI-edited and how, what is a real photograph, and one thing you refused to generate along with the reason you refused. If putting an image into that list makes you uneasy, the list is doing its job, and that image is the one to replace.

quiz.prompt: Kaye has an approved square graphic for a milk tea shop in Bacolod. At 9pm the client asks for the same promo in the tall placement as well, needed tomorrow. Kaye already has the brand template set built. What does she do?

options.text: Stretch the square file to the taller shape, since the elements and the brand colours all stay where the client approved them.
Rebuild the idea in the tall shape using the template, re-ranking the elements and dropping a line that was never essential.
Centre the square inside the tall frame and fill the space above and below it with a band in the shop's main brand colour.
Export the square again at the largest size the tool offers, so the placement has enough detail to crop the graphic itself.

quiz.explanation: A different shape is a different layout, not the same file resized. Stretching distorts the logo and the cup; padding with bars reads as a square somebody could not be bothered to rebuild; a bigger export does not change the shape. The template exists so that rebuilding means placing known parts again, which is a short job.

quiz.prompt: Jayson is designing a tarpaulin for a fun run in Los Banos. He has last year's tarp file, which was printed by a different shop, and the design is due tomorrow. What is the first move?

options.text: Reuse last year's setup, since tarpaulin printing is standard enough that one shop's file will work at another shop.
Set the file to the finished size at 300 dpi, the figure designers repeat for print, then send it to the shop.
Design it at screen size first for client approval, then ask the printer to scale the approved file up for the run.
Message the new printer for their own current requirements, keep the reply, and then design to exactly what it says.

quiz.explanation: Every printer has its own sheet: finished size, bleed beyond the trim, file type, colour handling, outlines. Last year's file encodes another shop's answers. 300 dpi is a rule of thumb built for something read at arm's length, not for a tarpaulin read from across a road, so the printer's own sheet decides. Ask, in writing, before designing.

quiz.prompt: Lorena puts the branch address and the promo cut-off date along the very bottom edge of a square graphic, because that strip of the photo is the emptiest part of the layout. What is the problem?

options.text: The outer band of a graphic gets covered by overlays and trimmed by crops, so essential details do not survive it.
Details like an address and a date should sit at the top left instead, because that is where a reader's eye starts.
An address and a date are fourth-rank detail, so they belong at a size small enough not to compete with the offer.
Nothing, as long as the type is large enough to stay readable at the size the graphic will appear in the feed.

quiz.explanation: Buttons, captions, profile bubbles and grid crops all eat the edges, and what they eat changes without warning. Keep essential content inside a safe-area guide and check the live placement yourself. Sizing the detail down is right and is not the fault here, and the top-left claim is a convention people repeat rather than a measured rule. The date does also need to exist as real text outside the image, as the next lesson says, and it still belongs on the graphic, because somebody who screenshots the post keeps only the image.

quiz.prompt: Aileen finishes a jobs-fair poster, views it in her design tool at fit-to-screen on a laptop, likes it, and sends it. What step did she skip that this chapter treats as non-negotiable?

options.text: Zooming to double size on the laptop so she can confirm the photo and the logo are both sharp enough to publish.
Asking the client to review it on their own device before anything is published, since it is their poster in the end.
Opening the exported file on a phone at real size with no zoom, then shrinking it to thumbnail to see what survives.
Checking the tool's built-in preview panel for the placement she chose, which shows how the design will be displayed.

quiz.explanation: A preview panel and a fit-to-screen laptop view are both kinder than reality. The check is the exported file, on a phone, at the size a reader gets, with no zoom, then shrunk to thumbnail to confirm the first-ranked element still leads. Client review is useful, but it is not a substitute for your own.

quiz.prompt: Rowena's clinic poster carries the whole weekly schedule as type inside the image, and it reads perfectly on a phone. A patient who uses a screen reader messages the page asking what the schedule is. What should have been done differently?

options.text: The schedule should also exist as real text in the caption or on the page, with alt text saying what the image is for.
The schedule should have been trimmed to three lines, since graphics carrying a lot of text get shown to fewer people.
Schedules change often, so the details belong in the caption where they are easier to edit after posting.
The schedule type should have been set larger than the headline, since legible on a laptop is not legible on a phone.

quiz.explanation: Type baked into a picture is part of the picture, so a screen reader and a browser with images off both get nothing from it. The fix is not to cut the schedule off the graphic: put the date, venue, deadline and contact in the caption or on the page as well, and write alt text describing what the image is for. The reach claim about text-heavy images is not something you can confirm, and the type was already legible, so size was not the fault.

quiz.prompt: A printing shop in Marikina asks Nico for an anniversary post showing customers lining up outside their store. There was no line. What does Nico do?

options.text: Build the queue from stock photos of people rather than generating it, since stock images are licensed.
Shoot the real shop, or drop the crowd entirely and let type and colour carry the anniversary offer instead.
Generate the queue and add an AI-generated label in the corner, which makes the use disclosed and so honest.
Shoot the shop on its busiest afternoon and generate a crowd behind it, so only the background is invented.

quiz.explanation: A queue of customers says something happened. It did not, so the image is a claim about demand, and no label rescues it: writing AI generated under an invented queue documents the claim rather than removing it. Generating only the crowd, or hiring licensed strangers to stand in it, invents the same event with tidier paperwork. Shoot the real thing, or let type and colour carry the offer.

quiz.prompt: Dianne's client wants a generated photo of the product on a plain background for a marketplace listing. The product is a real bag the buyer will receive in the post. Where is the line?

options.text: Generate it, since the listing already carries a written description of the actual bag's size and material.
Publish a generated photo and a phone snap of the real bag together, so a buyer can compare the two.
Ask the client to check the generated version against the real bag, then publish whichever one she approves.
Shoot the real bag and use AI only to clean the background, because the buyer will hold the thing itself.

quiz.explanation: If a customer will hold the real thing next to the picture, do not generate the picture. A listing photo is the buyer's evidence of what arrives, and a written description, a client's approval, or an honest second photo sitting beside it do not turn an invented product shot into a record. Shoot the bag on a table near a window and let the tool clean up the background.

quiz.prompt: Rina delivers twelve assets. On three of them she used background removal and generated a texture behind the type; the rest use the client's own photos. What does the handover carry?

options.text: A general line saying some AI editing tools were used in production, which covers the batch without listing assets.
Nothing on this, since the client reviewed and approved all twelve visuals before they were exported and delivered.
A per-asset note of what was generated, what was AI-edited and how, and which images are the client's real photos.
A note on the generated texture only, because removing a background edits a real photo rather than inventing one.

quiz.explanation: Disclosure to the client is per asset and specific, so they can answer for the work later without asking you. A vague batch line is not usable, approval of the look is not agreement about method, and background removal is still an edit the client may need to know about when the photo is reused elsewhere.

assignment.title: One idea, three places it lands
assignment.brief_mdx:
Pick one real Philippine small business you could plausibly work with: a milk tea shop, a barbershop, a dental clinic, an online thrift seller, the printing shop down the street. Look at what they already post and what they already print. Then build one small asset set from a single idea, and write up every decision inside it.

**What you make: three pieces, one idea.**

1. One graphic in the shape that business uses for its main screen placement.
2. One vertical version of the same idea, rebuilt rather than stretched.
3. One piece that leaves the screen: a tarpaulin, a flyer, a printed price list or a menu.

Put all three behind one publicly viewable link and paste that link in the link field. Open it yourself in a private browser window first. A reviewer with no account has to be able to see the files, and a link that asks them to request access is a failed submission.

The visuals are not marked on polish. The writing is the graded part.

**What you write: roughly 700 to 900 words.**

1. **The brief.** Four lines: who this is for, the one thing it has to say, what you want them to do, and where it will be seen. Then state the one message in a single sentence.
2. **The ranking.** What gets read first, second and third, and which of size, weight, position or colour you used to make that happen. Name what you pushed down to fourth.
3. **Type and colour.** Your type pairing and the reason for it. Your three colour roles: dominant, supporting, and an accent that appears rarely, plus what the accent means when it shows up. Then state that you checked text against background with a contrast checker instead of trusting your eye, and name the checker you used.
4. **The rebuild.** What changed between the screen shape and the vertical version, and why. Name the crop or safe-area risk that drove the change. If nothing changed, you padded it, and this section fails.
5. **Where you looked it up.** Name the source you used for the current spec of the screen placement, and the source of the printer's requirements for the physical piece, each with the date you checked it. Name the source, do not copy the number into your write-up. Any figure printed in a course is stale the month after.
6. **The template plan.** What stays fixed and what changes for the next ten assets, plus the file naming you would use so this client, or whoever replaces you, can find a file a year from now.
7. **AI disclosure.** Exactly what was generated or AI-edited, exactly what was not, and one thing you deliberately refused to generate, with the reason you refused.

**Two rules for the assets themselves.**

Put no price, promo, discount, opening time or claim on a graphic unless the business has already published it. If you use one, say in your write-up where you found it. Invented details about a real business fail the submission outright. If the layout needs a price to make sense, use one the business has already published, or leave an obvious placeholder.

Check each piece at the size it will really be seen. The screen pieces on a phone, held the way a person holds a phone. The physical piece printed, or at least viewed at the distance it will be read from. Anything essential you cannot read there is not finished yet.
criteria: The link opens for a reviewer with no account and holds three pieces built from one idea: the screen shape, the vertical, and one piece that leaves the screen, with the essential information on each legible at the size it would actually be seen
The vertical is rebuilt rather than stretched or padded, and the write-up names the crop or safe-area risk that drove what changed

The four-line brief is present, the one message is stated in one sentence, and the write-up names what is read first, second and third and which of size, weight, position or colour achieved that ranking
The type pairing and all three colour roles each carry a reason, and the learner states that contrast was checked with a named contrast checker rather than by eye

The screen placement spec and the printer requirements are each credited to a named source with the date it was checked, and every price, promo, time or claim on the assets is traced to something the business itself published, with nothing invented

The AI disclosure names what was generated or AI-edited, what was not, and one thing deliberately not generated with a reason, and the template plan names what stays fixed, what changes for the next ten assets, and the file naming
